questions.answer: Δp = ρgΔh, where Δh is the vertical depth difference between the two levels.
accepted_alternatives: Accept p₂ - p₁ = ρg(h₂ - h₁) with a consistent choice of the deeper level.
questions.unit_policy: No numerical unit is required, but Δh must be described as a vertical depth difference.
questions.tolerance: Both the relationship and the meaning of Δh are required.

marking_points.text: States Δp = ρgΔh
Identifies Δh as the vertical depth difference between the two levels
Selects A: the force is vertically downward and normal to the top patch

option_feedback.A: Correct. A fluid pressure force acts normal to the surface and into the object, so it is downward on a horizontal top patch.
option_feedback.B: Upward is the direction of the force on a horizontal bottom patch, not a top patch.
option_feedback.C: Pressure force is normal to a surface, not along it.
option_feedback.D: The local pressure-force direction is set by the surface orientation, not by the object's possible motion.

marking_points.text: Selects C: matching areas at matching depths experience equal forces in opposite directions

option_feedback.A: Fluid pressure acts on vertical as well as horizontal surfaces.
option_feedback.B: Matching points are at the same depth, and the forces point toward the block from opposite sides.
option_feedback.C: Correct. Equal pressure on equal matching areas gives equal and opposite horizontal forces.
option_feedback.D: An upward force does not remove horizontal forces; cancellation occurs between the opposite side forces themselves.

marking_points.text: Selects B: the deeper bottom face has the larger pressure force, so the vertical resultant is upward

option_feedback.A: Pressure increases rather than decreases with depth, so the top force is not the larger one.
option_feedback.B: Correct. Equal areas convert the greater bottom pressure into a greater upward force.
option_feedback.C: Equal area does not mean equal force when the pressures differ.
option_feedback.D: The top and bottom forces create the vertical difference; the symmetric side forces cancel horizontally.

questions.answer: Water pushes downward on the top face and upward on the bottom face. Matching side forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel horizontally. The remaining fluid-force resultant is the upward upthrust.
questions.tolerance: Directions and the pressure-force cause must be explicit.

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The force on the top face is vertically downward; the force on the bottom face is vertically upward.
accepted_alternatives: Accept forces described as normal to each face and directed into the case.
parts.tolerance: One mark for each face direction.

marking_points.text: States that the water force on the horizontal top face is vertically downward
States that the water force on the horizontal bottom face is vertically upward

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: At each matching depth the pressure is the same on both equal side areas, so the forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
accepted_alternatives: Accept an explanation based on pairing equal small areas at the same depth.
parts.tolerance: Both equality and opposite direction are required.

marking_points.text: Explains that matching equal side areas at the same depth experience equal pressure and equal force
States that the two horizontal side forces act in opposite directions and therefore cancel

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: The resultant fluid force is upward and is called upthrust.
parts.tolerance: Both direction and name are required for the mark.

marking_points.text: Identifies the resultant as an upward upthrust

questions.answer: Δp = 850 × 9.81 × 0.18 = 1.50 × 10³ Pa. The force difference is ΔF = ΔpA = 1.50093 × 10³ × 0.024 = 36.0 N upward.
questions.unit_policy: Pressure difference requires Pa and force difference requires N.
questions.tolerance: Accept 1.50 × 10³ Pa within 2 Pa and 36.0 N within 0.1 N, including consistent unrounded working.

marking_points.text: Uses Δp = ρgΔh with 850 kg m^-3, 9.81 N kg^-1 and 0.18 m
Obtains a pressure difference of 1.50 × 10^3 Pa with a suitable unit

parts.label: (b)
accepted_alternatives: Accept separate calculation of bottom and top forces followed by subtraction if the same 36.0 N difference is obtained.

marking_points.text: Uses the force difference ΔF = ΔpA with the common face area 0.024 m²
Obtains a pressure-force difference of 36.0 N with a suitable unit

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: The bottom face is deeper, so its upward pressure force is larger than the downward pressure force on the top face.
parts.tolerance: Require both the larger lower force and the upward direction.

marking_points.text: Explains that the deeper bottom face has the larger pressure force, so the force difference acts upward

questions.answer: The plate-level pressure difference is 2.45 × 10³ Pa. Because the plate areas differ and the sloping walls have vertical pressure-force components, Δp times one plate area is incomplete. Horizontal side components cancel, while their vertical components reinforce upward. Combining all normal pressure forces gives an upward resultant because lower regions experience greater hydrostatic pressure.
questions.unit_policy: The pressure difference requires Pa; explanation parts require no unit.
questions.tolerance: Do not credit use of a displaced-volume equation as a substitute for the requested pressure-force argument.

marking_points.text: Finds the vertical depth difference as 0.25 m and uses Δp = ρgΔh
Obtains a pressure difference of 2.45 × 10^3 Pa with a suitable unit

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: The top and bottom plate areas are unequal, so their forces are p_top A_top and p_bottom A_bottom rather than a common area times a pressure difference. The sloping walls also have vertical pressure-force components that contribute to the resultant.
parts.tolerance: Both unequal plate areas and side-wall contribution are required.

marking_points.text: Explains that unequal top and bottom areas prevent the two plate forces being written as one common area times Δp
Recognises that vertical components of pressure force on the sloping side walls also contribute to the complete upthrust

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: At matching depths, the horizontal components on the two symmetric walls are equal and opposite, so they cancel. Their vertical components both act upward and therefore add.
parts.tolerance: Horizontal and vertical component behavior must be distinguished.

marking_points.text: States that equal and opposite horizontal components from matching side-wall patches cancel
States that the vertical components from the two sloping walls act upward and add

parts.label: (d)
parts.answer: Pressure is greater on the deeper parts of the closed surface. When all normal pressure forces are combined, the lower and sloping-surface upward contributions exceed the downward contribution on the upper surface, leaving an upward resultant called upthrust.
parts.tolerance: Require the depth-pressure cause and the whole-surface upward resultant.

marking_points.text: Links greater depth on lower regions to greater hydrostatic pressure and stronger pressure-force contributions
Concludes that combining all normal pressure forces on the closed surface gives an upward resultant called upthrust
